title: Infra: GPU fleet, capacity, networking, IaC & CI/CD (team wiki)
author: Asha Raman
content:
Overview

This team-wiki page consolidates operational guidance, architecture decisions, and runbooks for Redwood's GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD pipelines for infra. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for provisioning and operating inference capacity.

Scope
- GPU fleet design and sizing guidance (on-demand, reserved, burst pools)
- Cloud account structure and VPC/networking patterns for inference clusters
- Terraform/IaC module catalog and usage examples for GPU infra
- CI/CD and build pipelines for infra modules and node images
- Runbooks for capacity incidents, node maintenance, and rollout/rollback

Owners and contacts
- Primary owners: Infra Engineering (infra-team@redwood.example.com)
- Fleet lead: Asha Raman (ashar@redwood.example.com)
- Capacity & planning: Miguel Ortega (miguel@redwood.example.com)
- Networking: Leila Chen (leilac@redwood.example.com)
- Oncall rotation: see /confluence/eng-infra/oncall-and-incident-response

Goals and SLOs
- Service availability for inference endpoints: 99.95% monthly for Dedicated and Private tiers.
- Median request latency p50 <= 20ms across short-sequence workloads on dedicated pools.
- Capacity provisioning lead time: automated scale-up within 10 minutes for on-demand burst pools, manual reserve provisioning <= 72 hours for reserved capacity.
- Cost target: keep per-token GPU cost growth <= 5% quarter-over-quarter through batching, caching, and quantization profiles.

Capacity planning fundamentals
1. Define workload classes
   - Latency-sensitive (interactive chat): prioritize low-latency pools, autoscale aggressively.
   - Throughput-oriented (batch embeddings): route to high-utilization pools with larger batch sizes.
   - Isolation-sensitive (regulated/private): private VPC only, reserved capacity.
2. Forecast inputs
   - Daily RPS by route and model
   - Average tokens per request and token generation rate
   - Hardware per-GPU throughput profile (tokens/sec) from benchmarking suite
   - Desired headroom (default 25% for autoscaling, configurable by pool)
3. Sizing formula (simplified)
   required_gpus = ceil((forecasted_tokens_per_sec / gpu_tokens_per_sec) * (1 + headroom))

Fleet architecture and pool types
- Dedicated pools: reserved instance fleets mapped to customers or internal tiers; predictable latency and throughput.
- Shared on-demand pools: high-utilization elastic pools with preemption and intelligent routing by policy.
- Burst pools: ephemeral capacity in cloud regions that can be spun up for short-lived traffic spikes.
- Cache-enabled fronting layer: autoscaler + request router that leverages prefix/KV caches to reduce downstream GPU work.

Instance types and placement (example table)
| Use case | Instance family | GPU | vCPU | Memory | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Low-latency interactive | nvidia-a100-80gb | A100-80GB | 32 | 768GB | Best for long-context models and KV cache heavy workloads |
| Cost-optimized throughput | nvidia-h100-80gb | H100-80GB | 64 | 1024GB | High throughput, preferred for batch & quantized models |
| Small models / dev | t4g | T4 | 8 | 64GB | For smoke testing and CI integration |

Note: exact instance families and SKUs are mapped in the infra inventory spreadsheet linked in related pages. Use the benchmark matrix in /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite for per-model throughput numbers.

Cloud accounts & networking patterns
- Account topology
  - Management account: central IAM, billing, audit logging, and shared services.
  - Infra accounts: per-region account for cluster infra (k8s control planes, autoscalers).
  - Customer/private accounts: customer-dedicated VPCs (private deployment).
- VPC design patterns
  - Separate subnets for control-plane, GPU nodes, and tooling/CI runners.
  - Egress via NAT gateways with proxy for outbound control-plane communications.
  - PrivateLink/endpoints for S3 and KMS to avoid public egress where required.
- Cross-account connectivity
  - Transit gateway for multi-region clusters or VPC peering for single-region setups.
  - Use cross-account IAM roles for automation with least-privilege.
- Network security
  - Node security groups: only allow control-plane ports and kubelet API from management subnets.
  - Cluster hardening: disable SSH from public internet; use bastion in management account.

Terraform / IaC modules
- Module catalog (high level)
  - module/gpu-cluster: provisions ASGs / node groups with GPU instance types, GPU drivers, and device plugins.
  - module/networking: VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT, endpoints.
  - module/iam-roles: cross-account roles and service principals for provisioning automation.
  - module/image-build: Packer/GC image builder for GPU node images.
  - module/monitoring: metrics, dashboards, and alerting scaffolding.

Module usage example (terraform)
```
module "gpu_cluster_us_east_1" {
  source           = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.example.com/infra/modules/gpu-cluster.git?ref=v1.8.0"
  region           = "us-east-1"
  cluster_name     = "inference-dedicated-us-east-1"
  instance_type    = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  min_size         = 4
  max_size         = 200
  gpu_drivers      = true
  taints           = ["dedicated=true:NoSchedule"]
  tags = {
    team = "infra"
    env  = "prod"
  }
}
```
Module development guidelines
- Semantic versioning of modules (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and changelogs required.
- All modules must include examples/, inputs.md, outputs.md and acceptance tests in terratest.
- PR checklist: terraform fmt, tflint, terratest passing, and documented migration steps.

CI/CD and build pipelines
- Pipeline types
  1. Module pipeline: validates and publishes terraform module versions to internal registry. Steps: fmt -> init -> plan (with stored state) -> terratest -> tag & release.
  2. Image build pipeline: Packer build for GPU node images -> image tests -> store AMI/GCR artifact -> publish hash in module inputs.
  3. Infra deploy pipeline: gated deploy to staging cluster (plan + apply with approval) -> canary deploy to prod using automated rollout policy.

Sample GitHub Actions snippet for module validation
```
name: terraform-module-ci
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  lint-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1
      - name: terraform fmt
        run: terraform fmt -check
      - name: terraform init
        run: terraform init
      - name: terraform validate
        run: terraform validate
      - name: run terratest
        run: make test
```
Gates and production safety
- Every module release must pass terratest and be smoke-tested in a staging account.
- Infra deploys to production must be approved by oncall or pool owner for changes affecting autoscaling, instance types, or network configs.

Runbooks (high level)
1) Capacity incident: "High GPU utilization / queue backlog"
   - Symptoms: pod Pending due to Insufficient resources, sustained GPU utilization > 85% for 15+ minutes, queue growth.
   - Immediate actions (0-10m):
     a) Notify #infra-oncall and open incident in PagerDuty.
     b) Check autoscaler logs and pending scale activities: `kubectl get nodes`, `kubectl top nodes`.
     c) If autoscaler failing, run manual scale: `terraform apply -var='min_size=...' -target=module.gpu_cluster.aws_autoscaling_group`.
   - Mitigation (10-60m):
     a) Shift non-critical jobs to batch pool using routing policy.
     b) Evacuate suspect nodes (cordon + drain) if hardware faults detected.
     c) Temporarily increase burst pool allocation in region (spin up new ASGs).
   - Post-incident (wiki): update forecast and increase headroom or tuning if recurring.

2) Node replacement (GPU OOM / driver crash)
   - Steps:
     1. Identify node: `kubectl describe node <node>` and check dmesg/journalctl for driver errors.
     2. Cordon: `kubectl cordon <node>`
     3. Drain: `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data`
     4. Replace instance in ASG or mark for lifecycle replacement.
     5. Validate: run smoke inference test against node and monitor logs.

3) Security or network outage
   - Follow playbook in /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security and notify security@redwood.example.com.

Operational checks and daily/weekly tasks
- Daily
  - Check critical alerts and PagerDuty queue.
  - Review autoscaler error metrics and reconcile failed scale events.
- Weekly
  - Capacity backlog review and ticketing for resizing/reserving.
  - Backfill AMI/image build pipeline if base images updated.
- Monthly
  - Update forecast model inputs and cross-check against billing spikes.

Change management and rollout checklist
1. Prepare change: update module, add migration notes if state changes required.
2. Run tests locally and in staging (terratest + smoke).
3. Open PR and request reviewers from reviewers list.
4. After approval: merge -> release module (tag) -> update infra deploy pipeline inputs.
5. Deploy to staging with `terraform plan/apply` and monitor.
6. Canary to prod: deploy to 5% of pools or one region first, monitor SLOs for 30-60 minutes before full rollout.
7. Rollback: documented terraform state restore steps in case of failure.

Appendix: useful commands and templates
- Terraform plan for a specific module\```
terraform init
terraform plan -target=module.gpu_cluster -var-file=env/prod.tfvars
\```
- Manual scale example\```
aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name inference-dedicated-us-east-1 --desired-capacity 50
\```
- Smoke test (local)\```
curl -s -X POST https://proxy-api.redwood.example.com/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"model":"small-test","input":"hello"}'
\```

Maintenance and lifecycle notes
- Module deprecation policy: major version bump + 45 days of overlap with migration guidance.
- Hardware refresh cadence: plan refresh for end-of-life GPU families every 18-24 months with pilot validation.

Glossary
- ASG: Auto Scaling Group
- AMI: Amazon Machine Image
- KV cache: key-value cache used to avoid re-computation of prefixes

If you find gaps or unclear steps, please create a PR against this page or contact the owners listed above.
